subject: chemistry_2
question_text: List out the uses of neon.

verification.note: Unit 10 (Noble Gases) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.89-90, the shaded sub-box "NOBLE GASES" of printed chapter 7; this question is printed on book p.89 as VSAQ 3. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK SHAPE: the printed answer gives exactly two uses, discharge tubes and fluorescent bulbs for advertisement display, and neon bulbs in botanical gardens and green houses. Both are kept. A third use, warning lights at airfields, is added because the question says "list out the uses" in the plural and two lines are thin for two marks. The orange-red colour of a neon discharge is added as the reason the first use exists; the book does not print it.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Discharge tubes and display lighting
lines: 1. Neon is used in discharge tubes and in
A neon discharge gives an orange-red glow,
which is why neon signs are used.
steps.why: Neon has a very high ionisation enthalpy, so a large voltage is needed to make it conduct; once it does, the excited atoms drop back and give out the orange-red light that a neon sign is named for. The gas is not used up, because it takes part in no chemical change.
common_mistakes: Writing that neon burns in the tube. Nothing burns; the gas glows because a current passes through it and does not react.
Giving a use of helium or argon instead. The electric bulb filling is argon, not neon.
steps.memory_tip: Neon is the sign-board gas: an orange-red glow in a glass tube.
steps.margin_note: Number your uses. An examiner marking a "list" question counts the numbered points.

steps.label: A second named use

lines.text: 2. Neon bulbs are used in botanical gardens

lines: 3. Neon lamps are used in warning lights at
steps.why: The greenhouse use is a lighting use as well: neon lamps give plants extra light without heating the air the way a filament lamp does. The airfield use rests on the colour, not on the chemistry, because long-wavelength red light is scattered least by fog droplets.
common_mistakes: Stopping at one use. The question asks for a list, so at least two numbered uses are needed.
Writing that neon is used as a cryogenic liquid. That is liquid helium, which boils at a far lower temperature.
steps.memory_tip: Three places to picture: a shop sign, a green house, and a runway light in fog.
steps.margin_note: Any two of these three uses complete the answer. The third is spare and costs one line.

insider_note: Two numbered uses are enough for full marks, so do not spend time on the physics of the discharge. Number them and stop.
